My Himalayan male cat developed a urinary blockage after being switched to a new food. We brought him in to have the crystals cleared, but before treatment could begin, the clinic required additional testing that significantly increased the cost. Between the diagnostic tests and treatment, we paid over $2,000. Some of the mandatory charges included thyroid testing, an administrative fee, and a STAT consult fee related to the X-rays, which felt excessive given the situation.

Dr. Anurova was knowledgeable and presented several treatment options. However, I felt there was a strong push toward hospitalization and more aggressive treatment. After discussing the options, we chose to have the crystals cleared and bring our cat home with medications and a prescription urinary diet rather than proceed with hospitalization.

Once home, we monitored him closely, fed him only wet food for a period of time, and followed all instructions. Each day he produced more urine, it appeared clear, and he gradually returned to normal. Thankfully, his recovery was smooth and he did not require hospitalization or surgery to widen the urethral opening.

While I was frustrated by the high cost, the mandatory fees, and what felt like pressure to choose a more expensive treatment plan, I am grateful that my cat recovered successfully. I appreciate that Dr. Anurova ultimately respected our decision and provided care that helped our cat make a full recovery without a more invasive procedure.

I brought my dog to this clinic because he had been coughing, and I left extremely disappointed with both the examination and the clinic’s lack of price transparency.

Before booking, I asked twice for the approximate cost of X-rays. Both times, they refused to give me even a general price range and said my dog had to be examined first.

The appointment cost $65 and lasted only about 3–5 minutes. The doctor looked at his gums and pressed on his throat once, which made him cough. I understand that coughing cannot always be diagnosed without X-rays or other tests, but I expected a much more thorough examination. This is not my first dog, and veterinary exams normally take longer. At minimum, I expected the doctor to carefully listen to his heart and lungs, assess his breathing and heart rate, and explain the possible causes.

Instead, I received almost no information and was simply given an estimate of approximately $600 for additional testing. The issue is not that veterinary care costs money. The issue is that I asked about the price twice, and they deliberately withheld even an approximate range. If they had answered my question honestly, I would not have booked the appointment.

The same thing happened six months ago when I asked about the cost of dental extractions: no price range, just another demand to pay for an examination first. After reading other reviews, it is clear that I am not the only client who has experienced this. Clients deserve upfront pricing and animals deserve more than a rushed, superficial examination.
